summary: Unexpected throttling observed when nightly CI deploys overlap with low-latency production traffic
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports repeated 429 responses for production low-latency API routes coinciding with nightly CI deployment window. Impact: Intermittent client-visible 429s for real-time endpoints (chat and streaming) lasting ~10-20 minutes during CI job fanout. Customer impact: degraded UX for paying users, spikes in support tickets.

Environment: Production (us-west-2) Dedicated pool assigned to FjordMaps (enterprise). Nightly CI: ~40 short-lived parallel agents that perform small model-serve health checks and a quick smoke-run of embedding imports.

Observed behavior: During overlap of CI job bursts and normal low-latency traffic, customer sees 5-15% of requests return 429s on realtime routes. Console shows burst credits dropping and per-route token windows briefly exhausted. Customer expected dedicated pool to isolate CI healthchecks from customer low-latency traffic and not bleed burst credits.

Expected behavior: Health-check / CI traffic should be accounted separately (or deprioritized) and not cause transient rate rejections for interactive routes at enterprise dedicated pool settings.
steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer runs nightly CI that spins up 30-50 short-lived agents performing healthcheck pings and 5-10 parallel quick embed uploads.
2) Simultaneously, send steady low-latency chat requests (small payloads, streaming) at baseline traffic (~200 rps).
3) Observe rate-limit headers and responses during CI job start (T+0 to T+5 minutes).

Notes: Repro is intermittent and depends on exact timing and ephemeral key usage patterns.

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: CI healthchecks are using ephemeral API keys and are being counted against the same burst pool/tenant window used by low-latency routes. Because the CI agents create many short-lived connections and quick embed writes, they consume burst credits and can push tenant refill below interactive thresholds.

What we checked:
- Console per-route token accounting (confirmed sudden dip in burst credits correlated with CI start).
- Token refill logs (no refill delays observed in control plane).
- Ingress proxy logs (ephemeral keys from same tenant showed high fanout).
- Autoscaler messages show pool was saturated briefly, causing some background warmups to queue.

Secondary hypothesis: Keepalive/health-checks from CI agents generate many small requests that trigger preflight/accounting path which counts differently than streaming requests, amplifying token consumption. Also possible route affinity was not correctly isolating CI route pattern, so rate-limiter treated them as interactive.

Next investigative steps:
- Request CI traffic sample headers from customer to validate api_key and route used.
- Check dedicated-pool config for isolated burst pools and priority lanes for enterprise customer.
- Rule out proxy connection reuse edge-case that double-counts tokens (see SUP-420069 and SUP-427801 for similar patterns).

resolution:
Workaround applied: Customer tagged CI keys with 'ci-' prefix and team enabled temporary low-priority background pool for tenant; immediate reduction of 429s on interactive routes observed. Recommended changes for customer: 1) stagger CI parallelism (reduce concurrent agents by ~50%), 2) use a separate service account with explicit low-priority/burst isolation for CI jobs, 3) configure per-route isolation for /v1/internal/* paths.

Long-term actions: Support to coordinate with Account Engineering to create a permanent burst-pool split on the customer's dedicated lease and update onboarding docs to flag ephemeral key patterns. Raised internal follow-up (INT-908776) to add a console check and runbook entry.

Status: Customer accepted workaround and requests Support to schedule permanent burst-pool separation. Keeping ticket open until permanent arrangement is completed.
